messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Doctor
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Violence: Violence, Authority Commands: Being given orders or instructions, Public Transport: Bus riding
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Thomas is a 63-year-old American physician who came to treatment after years of trying to keep his distress contained within the routines of work and home. He is married and has spent most of his adult life in medicine, a role that once gave him a sense of steadiness and competence. The event he returns to when he begins to describe what changed was a terrorist attack that unfolded during an ordinary commute on a city bus. What had begun as a familiar ride became, in his mind, the moment the ordinary world revealed itself as exposed and deceptive. He remembers the abrupt eruption of violence inside the confined space of the bus, the shock of seeing people turn from fellow passengers into possible threats, and the way shouted commands cut through the chaos. It is those elements that remain most charged for him now: the violence itself, the barked instructions, the feeling of being trapped on public transport with no control over what would happen next.

In the months afterward, Thomas found that the attack did not stay in the past as a completed event. He became acutely attentive to signs that danger might be approaching, especially in places that should have felt safe. At home, he began listening for small sounds that might mean someone was entering the house. A shift in the floorboards, a noise at the back door, an unfamiliar sound outside at night would pull his attention immediately. Even in his own living room he felt on guard, as if safety could not be assumed and had to be actively monitored. He described this not as caution but as necessity; in his view, the world had shown him what it really was, and relaxing would be foolish.

His thinking about other people changed as well. Thomas had come to believe that people are not what they seem. On the bus that day, strangers had become frighteningly unpredictable, and since then he has carried a persistent distrust into everyday encounters. He notices himself studying faces, tones of voice, the slightest edge in someone’s manner. He no longer assumes benign intent. In crowded settings he finds himself wondering who might suddenly become violent, who might be concealing something, who might issue orders that demand instant obedience. He is certain now that the world is dangerous, and he says this with the conviction of someone who feels he has learned a hard truth rather than developed a fear. Alongside this is a heavier conclusion: that his life has been destroyed by the trauma. He speaks of it not dramatically but flatly, as a settled fact that divides his life into before and after.

These changes have shown up sharply in his work as a doctor. Hospitals are hierarchical places, full of instructions, brief commands, and urgent exchanges, and Thomas finds that being given orders or even routine directives can provoke a sudden internal jolt. A curt instruction from an administrator, a forceful request during a tense clinical moment, or a raised voice in a hallway can leave him bristling and angry before he has fully registered why. He has become more irritable with colleagues and staff, quicker to snap, less able to absorb the pressures of the day without reacting. He is aware that his angry outbursts are affecting how others experience him. At home, his wife has also felt the change. He is more easily set off, more guarded, and less able to let small frustrations pass. What she may experience as ordinary household noise, he hears first as a possible sign of intrusion.

Over time he also reshaped his daily life around what he could not tolerate. He stopped riding buses altogether. He tells himself there is no reason to place himself back into that kind of enclosed vulnerability, and he has reorganized his routines accordingly. The avoidance is practical on the surface, but it has narrowed his world. He drives when he can, plans carefully, and declines situations that would require public transport. The result has been more strain, more rigidity, and a life that feels progressively smaller than the one he had before.

By the time Thomas sought help, the burden of living in this constant state of vigilance had become harder to disguise. He was troubled by how often he was scanning for danger in his own home and by how much anger now sat close to the surface. He was also unsettled by the bleakness of his own conclusions about life and other people. What finally brought him in was not a single crisis so much as the recognition that this way of living had become his new normal. He fears that the attack took from him the ability to feel safe anywhere and that this is permanent. At the same time, he still hopes there might be some way to live without always listening for the next threat.
